title: Interviews & Portraits
subtitle: Conduct a sharp interview, sketch a faithful portrait, and weave quotes into your writing

lessons.title: Mener un entretien
lessons.description: Prepare a real interview, ask questions that open doors rather than close them, and let silence do some of the work.

blocks.heading: Préparer avant de poser une seule question
blocks.body: A good interview is decided largely before it begins. The interviewer who arrives with a clear guide d'entretien — a small set of questions ordered from broad to specific — can afford to abandon it the moment something more interesting comes up. Improvisation works only once the groundwork has already been laid.

examples.french: Un bon entretien se prépare bien avant la première question.
examples.english: A good interview is prepared long before the first question.

examples.french: Elle arrive toujours avec un guide d'entretien, qu'elle n'ouvre presque jamais.
examples.english: She always arrives with an interview guide, which she almost never opens.

examples.french: Il faut savoir ce que l'on cherche avant de savoir ce que l'on va demander.
examples.english: You must know what you are looking for before you know what you will ask.

examples.french: La préparation ne sert pas à tout prévoir, mais à pouvoir tout accueillir.
examples.english: Preparation is not there to foresee everything, but to be able to welcome anything.

blocks.tip: Order your questions from the general to the specific — starting narrow forces the conversation into a corner it may never leave.

blocks.heading: Ouvrir, relancer, creuser
blocks.body: A closed question invites a single word; an open question invites a story. The best interviewers lean on open questions to start, then use relances — short follow-ups like 'c'est-à-dire ?' or 'pouvez-vous préciser ?' — to dig past the first, rehearsed answer into something the person had not planned to say.

examples.french: Une question fermée obtient un fait ; une question ouverte obtient un récit.
examples.english: A closed question gets a fact; an open question gets a story.

examples.french: Je rebondis toujours sur le dernier mot, jamais sur ma prochaine question.
examples.english: I always pick up on the last word, never on my next question.

examples.french: Creusons cette réponse : qu'entendez-vous exactement par là ?
examples.english: Let's dig into that answer: what exactly do you mean by that?

examples.french: Une bonne relance ne dirige pas la réponse, elle l'invite.
examples.english: A good follow-up does not steer the answer, it invites it.

blocks.tip: 'Pourquoi' can sound like an accusation; 'qu'est-ce qui vous a amené à...' asks the same thing without putting anyone on the defensive.

blocks.heading: Écouter, se taire, laisser le silence travailler
blocks.body: Inexperienced interviewers rush to fill every gap; experienced ones let a silence stretch a second or two past what feels comfortable, because that is often when the most honest sentence arrives. When an answer visibly dodges the question, the tool is not aggression but a calm, precise recadrage — bringing the conversation back, once, without a fight.

examples.french: L'écoute active demande de se taire plus souvent qu'on ne le croit.
examples.english: Active listening requires staying silent more often than one might think.

examples.french: Il a laissé le silence s'installer, et elle a fini par répondre vraiment.
examples.english: He let the silence settle, and she finally gave a real answer.

examples.french: Quand on élude une question, mieux vaut recadrer une fois que couper la parole.
examples.english: When a question is dodged, it is better to reframe once than to interrupt.

examples.french: Je ne coupe jamais la parole ; je reviens, calmement, à ma question.
examples.english: I never cut people off; I calmly return to my question.

blocks.tip: If a source esquive twice on the same point, name it gently: 'je remarque que vous n'avez pas répondu sur ce point précis' — naming the dodge is often enough to end it.

blocks.heading: L'interrogation soutenue — l'inversion complexe
blocks.body: Formal French interviewing favours inversion over 'est-ce que': 'Quels sont, selon vous, les enjeux ?' sounds more measured than 'Qu'est-ce que vous pensez que...'. When the subject is a noun rather than a pronoun, French repeats it as a pronoun after the verb — the 'inversion complexe' — which lets a long, precise subject stay in its natural place at the front of the sentence.

examples.french: Quels sont, selon vous, les enjeux réels de ce dossier ?
examples.english: What, in your view, are the real stakes of this matter?

examples.french: Diriez-vous que cette décision marque un tournant ?
examples.english: Would you say this decision marks a turning point?

examples.french: Le gouvernement a-t-il anticipé cette réaction ?
examples.english: Did the government anticipate this reaction?

examples.french: Pourriez-vous revenir sur les circonstances exactes de cette rencontre ?
examples.english: Could you go back over the exact circumstances of this meeting?

blocks.tip: 'Le gouvernement a-t-il anticipé...' repeats the noun subject ('le gouvernement') as a pronoun ('il') after the verb — dropping the pronoun and inverting the noun directly ('a le gouvernement anticipé') is simply not correct French.

blocks.heading: Le discours indirect pour rapporter une question
blocks.body: Writing up an interview later means converting the live questions into reported speech, and the interrogative words change shape when they do: 'qu'est-ce que' becomes 'ce que', 'qu'est-ce qui' becomes 'ce qui', and a yes/no question introduced by 'est-ce que' is reported with 'si'. Tenses shift back one step under the usual concordance des temps.

examples.french: Je lui ai demandé ce qu'il pensait de cette réforme.
examples.english: I asked him what he thought of this reform.

examples.french: Je voulais savoir si elle regrettait sa décision.
examples.english: I wanted to know whether she regretted her decision.

examples.french: Elle m'a demandé pourquoi je posais cette question précise.
examples.english: She asked me why I was asking that particular question.

examples.french: Je lui ai demandé ce qui l'avait poussé à accepter cet entretien.
examples.english: I asked him what had prompted him to agree to this interview.

blocks.tip: Never carry 'est-ce que' or 'qu'est-ce que' into reported speech — 'je lui ai demandé qu'est-ce qu'il pensait' is a common error; the reported form is always 'ce que'.

passages.title: L'entretien avec Aïcha Diallo
passages.french:
Nadia Ferrand n'avait que vingt-cinq minutes pour interviewer Aïcha Diallo, l'ingénieure qui venait de démissionner avec fracas de son poste chez Solvenia.
Elle avait préparé un guide d'entretien de quinze questions. Elle n'en posa que six.
« Pourquoi partir maintenant, alors que le projet touche presque à sa fin ? » commença Nadia, d'une voix volontairement neutre.
Aïcha hésita, regarda la table, puis répondit d'un ton mesuré : « Parce que finir un projet dont on ne croit plus au sens ne me semblait pas être un acte de loyauté, mais un acte de confort. »
Nadia laissa un silence de quelques secondes, sans relancer.
« Vous pouvez préciser ce que vous entendez par « un acte de confort » ? » reprit-elle enfin, doucement.
Aïcha soupira, puis se livra pour la première fois : « Rester m'aurait évité d'avoir à me justifier. Partir m'oblige à le faire, ici, devant vous. »
À un moment, une question sembla la déstabiliser : « Regrettez-vous d'avoir attendu si longtemps ? »
Elle élusa d'abord, parlant du contexte général de l'entreprise. Nadia n'insista pas immédiatement ; elle rebondit sur un détail cité en passant, deux minutes plus tôt.
« Vous avez mentionné une réunion de mars. Que s'est-il passé, exactement, ce jour-là ? »
Cette fois, Aïcha répondit sans détour, et l'entretien changea de nature.
À la fin, Nadia referma son carnet sans avoir eu besoin de ses neuf dernières questions. Le fil conducteur s'était trouvé tout seul, quelque part entre un silence et une relance.
passages.english:
Nadia Ferrand had only twenty-five minutes to interview Aïcha Diallo, the engineer who had just resigned in dramatic fashion from her position at Solvenia.
She had prepared an interview guide of fifteen questions. She asked only six.
"Why leave now, when the project is almost finished?" Nadia began, in a deliberately neutral voice.
Aïcha hesitated, looked at the table, then answered in a measured tone: "Because finishing a project I no longer believed in didn't strike me as an act of loyalty, but an act of comfort."
Nadia let a few seconds of silence pass, without prompting further.
"Could you clarify what you mean by 'an act of comfort'?" she finally said, gently.
Aïcha sighed, then opened up for the first time: "Staying would have spared me from having to justify myself. Leaving forces me to do it, here, in front of you."
At one point, a question seemed to unsettle her: "Do you regret having waited so long?"
She dodged at first, talking about the company's general context. Nadia did not press immediately; she picked up on a detail mentioned in passing two minutes earlier.
"You mentioned a meeting in March. What exactly happened that day?"
This time, Aïcha answered without evasion, and the interview changed in nature.
At the end, Nadia closed her notebook without having needed her last nine questions. The throughline had found itself, somewhere between a silence and a follow-up.

lessons.title: Le portrait journalistique
lessons.description: Build a written portrait around telling details and scene, not a résumé — fair to its subject, honest about its own point of view.

blocks.heading: Choisir le détail qui parle
blocks.body: A journalistic portrait is not a biography squeezed into fewer words — it is built on a handful of well-chosen details that reveal more than a paragraph of description could. A worn watch, a habit of finishing other people's sentences, the way someone answers before a question is fully asked: these details carry the portrait, while raw facts merely support it.

examples.french: Un bon portrait tient sur trois détails, pas sur trente adjectifs.
examples.english: A good portrait rests on three details, not thirty adjectives.

examples.french: Elle portait la même montre cassée depuis quinze ans ; personne n'a jamais osé le lui demander.
examples.english: She had worn the same broken watch for fifteen years; no one ever dared ask her about it.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas ce qu'il dit qui le trahit, c'est la façon dont il finit vos phrases.
examples.english: It is not what he says that gives him away, it is the way he finishes your sentences.

examples.french: Un détail révélateur en dit plus long qu'une liste de qualités.
examples.english: One revealing detail says more than a list of qualities.

blocks.tip: Show, don't tell: instead of writing 'elle est impatiente', write the detail that proves it — the reader will supply the adjective on their own, and trust it more.

blocks.heading: Mélanger scène et biographie
blocks.body: A strong profile alternates between scene — a moment happening in real time, with dialogue and gesture — and biography — the compressed background the reader needs to understand the scene's stakes. Pure biography reads like a CV; pure scene leaves the reader lost. The skill is in the cutting between the two.

examples.french: La scène d'ouverture capte l'attention ; la biographie, glissée juste après, l'explique.
examples.english: The opening scene grabs attention; the biography, slipped in right after, explains it.

examples.french: On campe le personnage en une scène avant de revenir vingt ans en arrière.
examples.english: You establish the character in one scene before going back twenty years.

examples.french: Trop de biographie d'un coup noie le lecteur ; il faut la distiller.
examples.english: Too much biography at once drowns the reader; it must be dispensed sparingly.

examples.french: Chaque retour en arrière doit se justifier par la scène qui l'a précédé.
examples.english: Every flashback must be justified by the scene that came before it.

blocks.tip: Open on a scene, not on a birth date — readers commit to a person before they commit to a timeline.

blocks.heading: Trouver un angle, éviter le cliché
blocks.body: Every subject has already been described a dozen predictable ways; the portraitist's job is to find the angle no one else used — not to distort the person, but to see past the obvious. Two failure modes bracket the honest portrait: l'hagiographie, which flatters until nothing rings true, and le portrait à charge, which punishes until nothing feels fair.

examples.french: Le premier cliché venu à l'esprit est presque toujours le mauvais angle.
examples.english: The first cliché that comes to mind is almost always the wrong angle.

examples.french: Un portrait complaisant ne rend service ni au lecteur ni au sujet.
examples.english: A fawning portrait does neither the reader nor the subject any favours.

examples.french: Un portrait à charge se lit vite, mais ne convainc jamais longtemps.
examples.english: A hit piece reads quickly, but never convinces for long.

examples.french: Le portrait le plus juste est souvent le plus nuancé, jamais le plus flatteur.
examples.english: The most accurate portrait is often the most nuanced one, never the most flattering.

blocks.tip: If you cannot imagine your subject disagreeing with a single line of your portrait, you have probably written flattery, not a portrait.

blocks.heading: L'imparfait descriptif et le passé simple narratif (reconnaissance)
blocks.body: Written portraits mix two past tenses with distinct jobs: the imparfait paints an ongoing state — what someone was like, what a room looked like, a recurring habit — while the passé simple marks a single, completed event pushing the narrative forward. You will rarely write the passé simple yourself outside literary exercises, but C1 readers must recognise it instantly in press profiles and literary portraits.

examples.french: Elle portait toujours la même montre cassée ; ce jour-là, elle l'ôta pour la première fois.
examples.english: She always wore the same broken watch; that day, she took it off for the first time.

examples.french: Il parlait peu, mais quand il prit la parole, la salle entière se tut.
examples.english: He spoke little, but when he took the floor, the whole room fell silent.

examples.french: La pièce sentait le café froid ; personne n'osa ouvrir la fenêtre.
examples.english: The room smelled of cold coffee; no one dared open the window.

examples.french: Elle hésitait souvent ; ce soir-là, pourtant, elle répondit sans un instant d'hésitation.
examples.english: She often hesitated; that evening, though, she answered without a moment's hesitation.

blocks.tip: Spot the passé simple by its distinctive endings ('-a', '-it', '-ut' in the third person singular: 'ôta', 'prit', 'tut') — recognising it is the C1 goal, not necessarily producing it in your own writing.

blocks.heading: Les propositions relatives pour caractériser
blocks.body: Relative clauses let a portrait pack detail into a single flowing sentence instead of a string of short, choppy ones. 'Qui', 'que', 'dont' and 'où' each attach a different kind of information to the person or thing just named — and choosing the right one, especially 'dont' for anything governed by 'de', is a mark of real fluency.

examples.french: C'est un homme dont on se souvient longtemps après l'avoir rencontré.
examples.english: He is a man one remembers long after meeting him.

examples.french: Le bureau qu'elle occupe depuis dix ans n'a jamais changé de place.
examples.english: The office she has occupied for ten years has never moved.

examples.french: L'école où il a grandi n'existe plus aujourd'hui.
examples.english: The school where he grew up no longer exists today.

examples.french: C'est une qualité dont peu de dirigeants peuvent se prévaloir.
examples.english: It is a quality few leaders can claim for themselves.

blocks.tip: 'Dont' replaces anything introduced by 'de' — 'une qualité dont il est fier' (fier DE), never 'une qualité que il est fier de', which stacks the preposition twice.

passages.title: Portrait : le silence de Julien Servaz
passages.french:
On l'appelle « le silencieux » depuis le lycée, et Julien Servaz, aujourd'hui chef étoilé, ne dément jamais ce surnom.
Sa cuisine, en revanche, parle pour lui. Ce soir-là, dans la salle presque vide de son restaurant, il finit chaque plat avant de lever les yeux vers la salle, jamais avant.
Son histoire, on la connaît en deux lignes : fils d'ouvriers, formé sur le tas, trois étoiles obtenues à trente-quatre ans. Mais ces deux lignes ne disent rien de l'essentiel.
Ce soir-là, un serveur renversa une carafe. Julien ne cria pas. Il ramassa lui-même les morceaux, en silence, pendant que la brigade retenait son souffle.
« Ce n'est pas de la sévérité, expliqua-t-il plus tard, dont on entendait à peine la voix. C'est que je n'ai jamais appris à élever le ton. Chez moi, on ne criait pas, on se taisait, et le silence disait tout. »
Ce silence, justement, est le fil conducteur de sa cuisine : des plats qui ne cherchent jamais à impressionner, mais qui s'imposent, un par un, sans un mot de trop.
On pourrait dresser un portrait flatteur de cet homme discret, presque austère. On pourrait tout aussi bien en dresser un féroce, tant son perfectionnisme épuise parfois son équipe.
La vérité, comme souvent, tient entre les deux : Julien Servaz est un homme dont l'exigence a un prix, que sa brigade dont plusieurs membres le suivent depuis quinze ans semble malgré tout disposée à payer.
À la fin du service, il éteignit les lumières de la cuisine une à une. Le silence, cette fois, n'appartenait qu'à lui.
passages.english:
He has been called "the silent one" since high school, and Julien Servaz, now a starred chef, never denies the nickname.
His cooking, however, speaks for him. That evening, in his restaurant's nearly empty dining room, he finished every plate before ever looking up at the room, never before.
His story is known in two lines: son of factory workers, trained on the job, three stars earned at thirty-four. But those two lines say nothing of the essential thing.
That evening, a waiter knocked over a carafe. Julien did not shout. He picked up the pieces himself, in silence, while the kitchen brigade held its breath.
"It's not severity," he explained later, his voice barely audible, "it's that I never learned to raise my voice. At home, we didn't shout, we went quiet, and the silence said everything."
That silence, precisely, is the throughline of his cooking: dishes that never try to impress, but assert themselves, one by one, without a single word too many.
One could paint a flattering portrait of this discreet, almost austere man. One could just as easily paint a harsh one, given how much his perfectionism sometimes exhausts his team.
The truth, as often, lies between the two: Julien Servaz is a man whose exacting standards come at a price, one his brigade — several of whom have followed him for fifteen years — nonetheless seems willing to pay.
At the end of service, he switched off the kitchen lights one by one. The silence, this time, belonged to him alone.

lessons.title: La citation
lessons.description: Choose the right quote, attribute it precisely, and integrate it into your own writing without distorting it.

blocks.heading: Choisir la citation qui mérite d'être une citation
blocks.body: Not every sentence a source says deserves quotation marks. A quote earns its place when the wording itself matters — a striking phrase, a precise admission, an unexpected turn — while ordinary information is better paraphrased in your own, tighter prose. Quoting everything drowns the one sentence that actually needed to stand out.

examples.french: On ne cite pas pour prouver qu'on était présent, mais parce que les mots comptent.
examples.english: You quote not to prove you were there, but because the words matter.

examples.french: Une citation banale n'a pas sa place entre guillemets ; paraphrasez-la.
examples.english: A banal statement has no place in quotation marks; paraphrase it.

examples.french: La meilleure citation est souvent la plus courte, jamais la plus complète.
examples.english: The best quote is often the shortest one, never the most complete.

examples.french: Une seule phrase bien choisie vaut mieux qu'un paragraphe entier retranscrit tel quel.
examples.english: One well-chosen sentence is worth more than an entire paragraph transcribed as is.

blocks.tip: Ask yourself: would this sentence lose something if I paraphrased it? If the answer is no, it does not need quotation marks.

blocks.heading: Rester fidèle sans être esclave du mot à mot
blocks.body: A direct quote must reproduce the exact words — no correcting the grammar, no smoothing an awkward phrase, no changing tense for convenience. But fidelity also means respecting context: trimming a quote with an ellipsis is honest only when what is cut does not reverse its meaning. Quoting accurately and quoting fairly are two separate obligations, both non-negotiable.

examples.french: On ne corrige jamais une citation, même maladroite ; on la choisit, ou on la laisse.
examples.english: You never correct a quote, even a clumsy one; you either choose it, or leave it out.

examples.french: Une citation tronquée sans malhonnêteté indique toujours ce qu'elle a coupé.
examples.english: A quote honestly trimmed always indicates what it has cut.

examples.french: Sortie de son contexte, une phrase peut dire presque l'inverse de ce qu'elle voulait dire.
examples.english: Taken out of context, a sentence can say almost the opposite of what it meant.

examples.french: La fidélité à la citation ne dispense jamais de vérifier la source.
examples.english: Faithfulness to a quote never excuses skipping the source check.

blocks.tip: Use an ellipsis in brackets — […] — to mark a cut inside a quote; an unmarked cut is not editing, it is misquotation.

blocks.heading: Varier les verbes, préciser le ton
blocks.body: 'Dire' works, but it flattens every quote to the same neutral tone. Choosing 'affirmer', 'concéder', 'reconnaître', 'souligner' or 'déplorer' tells the reader something the words alone do not: whether the speaker was certain, reluctant, insistent, or regretful. The verb introducing a quote is itself a small act of interpretation — use it honestly.

examples.french: « Nous avons sous-estimé le problème », a-t-elle reconnu, presque à voix basse.
examples.english: "We underestimated the problem," she acknowledged, almost under her breath.

examples.french: « Cette décision reste la bonne », a-t-il martelé, sans une once de doute apparent.
examples.english: "This decision remains the right one," he hammered home, without a trace of apparent doubt.

examples.french: « Je le concède volontiers », a-t-elle ajouté, avant de nuancer aussitôt son propos.
examples.english: "I gladly concede that," she added, before immediately qualifying her statement.

examples.french: Le verbe introducteur choisi en dit parfois plus long que la citation elle-même.
examples.english: The chosen reporting verb sometimes reveals more than the quote itself.

blocks.tip: Never let the reporting verb editorialise beyond what the tone actually supports — writing 'a-t-il menti' instead of 'a-t-il affirmé' turns reporting into an accusation.

blocks.heading: Le discours rapporté et la concordance des temps
blocks.body: Converting a direct quote into indirect speech shifts its tense back one step whenever the reporting verb is in the past: présent becomes imparfait, passé composé becomes plus-que-parfait, futur becomes conditionnel présent. Pronouns and possessives shift too — 'je' and 'mon' in the original quote become 'il/elle' and 'son' once folded into someone else's sentence.

examples.french: « Je regrette ma décision » devient : elle a dit qu'elle regrettait sa décision.
examples.english: "I regret my decision" becomes: she said she regretted her decision.

examples.french: « Nous avons terminé » devient : ils ont affirmé qu'ils avaient terminé.
examples.english: "We have finished" becomes: they stated they had finished.

examples.french: « Je reviendrai demain » devient : il a promis qu'il reviendrait le lendemain.
examples.english: "I will come back tomorrow" becomes: he promised he would come back the next day.

examples.french: « C'est déjà réglé » devient : elle a précisé que c'était déjà réglé.
examples.english: "It is already settled" becomes: she specified that it was already settled.

blocks.tip: Time markers shift too: 'demain' becomes 'le lendemain', 'hier' becomes 'la veille' — forgetting this is the most common mistake when converting a live quote into a written account.

blocks.heading: L'inversion du sujet dans l'incise
blocks.body: When an attribution clause follows a direct quote, French inverts the subject and verb: 'dit-il', 'répondit-elle', 'précisa-t-il' — never 'il dit' in that position. A '-t-' is inserted between two vowels for pronunciation ('a-t-elle dit'). Varying the verb across a piece — 'reprit', 'ajouta', 'conclut' instead of repeating 'dit' — keeps a long quoted exchange readable.

passages.title: Une phrase, deux articles
passages.french:
Le maire de Verrières avait dit une seule phrase, lors d'un conseil municipal filmé : « Nous n'avons pas les moyens de tout faire tout de suite, et il faudra sans doute renoncer à certains projets. »
Le lendemain, deux journaux locaux la citèrent, chacun à sa manière.
Le premier titra : « Le maire renonce à ses projets », et ne retint que la fin de la phrase, entre guillemets, sans l'ellipse qui aurait signalé la coupe.
Le second choisit de citer la phrase intégralement, puis d'ajouter, en contexte : « Une déclaration prononcée en réponse à une question sur le budget, et non une annonce spontanée. »
Amandine Roussel, rédactrice en chef du second journal, reçut un appel furieux du premier rédacteur, qui l'accusait de vouloir défendre le maire.
« Je ne le défends pas, répondit-elle calmement. Je cite la phrase entière, avec son contexte. Vous, vous avez tronqué la citation sans le signaler, et le sens en est presque inversé. »
« Les lecteurs veulent des titres courts », rétorqua l'autre, un peu sur la défensive.
« Un titre court n'oblige pas à déformer les propos de quelqu'un, reprit Amandine. On peut être bref et rester fidèle. »
Le maire, contacté à son tour, se contenta de déplorer : « Je ne reconnais pas mes propos dans ce premier article. Le second, en revanche, dit exactement ce que j'ai voulu dire. »
Amandine referma le dossier ce soir-là avec une certitude simple : une bonne citation ne se juge jamais à sa longueur, mais à ce qu'elle laisse, ou non, deviner de son contexte.
passages.english:
The mayor of Verrières had said a single sentence, during a filmed town council meeting: "We do not have the means to do everything at once, and we will probably have to give up on some projects."
The next day, two local papers quoted it, each in its own way.
The first ran the headline "Mayor abandons his projects," keeping only the end of the sentence, in quotation marks, without the ellipsis that would have flagged the cut.
The second chose to quote the sentence in full, then add, for context: "A statement made in response to a question about the budget, not a spontaneous announcement."
Amandine Roussel, editor-in-chief of the second paper, received an angry call from the first paper's editor, who accused her of trying to defend the mayor.
"I am not defending him," she replied calmly. "I am quoting the whole sentence, with its context. You truncated the quote without flagging it, and the meaning is almost reversed as a result."
"Readers want short headlines," the other retorted, somewhat defensively.
"A short headline does not require distorting someone's words," Amandine went on. "You can be brief and still stay faithful."
The mayor, contacted in turn, simply lamented: "I do not recognise my own words in that first article. The second one, however, says exactly what I meant to say."
Amandine closed the file that evening with one simple certainty: a good quote is never judged by its length, but by what it does, or does not, let the reader guess about its context.
